questions.q: According to DAMA's Data Management Body of Knowledge (DMBOK), what is data quality?
options: The degree to which data is fit for its intended purpose(s)
The percentage of fields in a table that are not NULL
The absence of any typos or formatting errors
The total number of rows that have been validated
questions.explain: DMBOK defines quality as fitness for use — relative to a specific purpose, not an absolute standard of perfection.

questions.q: Why can the exact same dataset be 'high quality' for one team and 'low quality' for another?
options: Because fitness for use is judged against each team's specific intended purpose, and purposes differ
Because data literally changes values depending on who queries it
Because only certified data engineers are allowed to judge quality
It can't — quality is a single fixed property of the data itself
questions.explain: A dataset fit for one purpose (e.g. a quick sales call) can be unfit for another (e.g. legal compliance) using the identical rows.

questions.q: A table of customer addresses is 100% complete and perfectly formatted, but half the ZIP codes belong to the wrong state. What does this demonstrate?
options: That completeness alone does not guarantee fitness for use — accuracy is a separate dimension
That the table is high quality because it has no missing values
That formatting is the only dimension that matters
That this table cannot be measured for quality at all
questions.explain: Completeness and accuracy are different dimensions; acing one doesn't mean the data is fit for a use that depends on the other.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the six data quality dimensions introduced in this lesson?
options: Popularity
Accuracy
Completeness
Timeliness
questions.explain: The six dimensions are accuracy, completeness, consistency, validity, uniqueness, and timeliness — popularity isn't one of them.

questions.q: Per this lesson, who is best positioned to judge whether data is 'fit for purpose'?
options: The people who actually use the data for a specific purpose
Whoever happens to own the database server
A single company-wide standard that applies to every dataset identically
No one — fitness for use cannot be judged
questions.explain: Fitness for use is a judgment call made relative to a specific, named use — made by the people who consume the data for that use, a topic Lesson 4 covers in depth.
